Here are practical things to check at the music store, based only on what we discussed earlier:

- Body & construction: try both Strat-style and Les Paul-style shapes. Les Pauls are mahogany bodies with a set neck and a carved maple top (heavier, lots of sustain); Strat-style bodies are contoured, usually bolt-on necks, and feel lighter and more ergonomic.

- Neck feel & profile: play several neck profiles to see what fits your hand. Les Paul necks (set neck) feel different from bolt-on Strat necks.

- Pickups & tonal options: compare single-coils vs humbuckers. Also try guitars with coil-tap or coil-splitting if you want more tonal flexibility (gives you both thicker humbucker tones and brighter single-coil-like tones).

- Strings & setup: check action and intonation; low action is easier to fret but can buzz if not set up right. If you plan to use lower or open tunings (like open D), consider heavier-gauge strings for fuller tone and better tension.

- Playability in different styles: plug the guitar in and play clean and overdriven settings. Les Pauls were recommended for rock/ thicker tones and have strong sustain; also test whether the guitar suits fingerpicking or acoustic-like parts if that’s important to you.

- Hardware & tuning stability: try bending and using the tremolo (if present) and check tuners and bridge for stability.

- Weight & balance: Les Pauls can be heavy—make sure it’s comfortable sitting and standing.

- Tone through your amp: bring or use the store amp and try amp settings you commonly use so you hear the guitar in realistic settings.

- Inspect cosmetics & electronics: look for any crackling from pots/switches and verify the finish and frets are in good shape.

A good approach: try a few guitars of different types (Strat vs Les Paul styles, different pickup configurations), play the songs/techniques you actually use (including any open tunings or fingerpicking), and compare feel, tone, and comfort before deciding.

Based on what you’ve already been asking about, a NAS makes sense if you want a more convenient, central backup for multiple devices and more storage than a single external drive. A few practical points from our earlier conversation to help you decide:

- Use case: If you need a central backup location for your laptop and phone now, a NAS will do that (works with Time Machine on Mac, Windows backup, and third-party backup tools).
- Security: Look for a NAS that supports encryption (e.g., AES-256), access control (ACLs, user permissions), and features like two-factor authentication — you raised these concerns earlier, and some models emphasize them. 
- Capacity/expandability: Choose 2-bay vs 4-bay based on how much storage and redundancy you want. 2-bay is cheaper and compact; 4-bay gives more drive capacity and RAID options for growth and resilience.
- Beginner-friendly models: You were interested in easy-to-use options — Synology models were mentioned as good beginner choices (example: DS218j as an affordable 2-bay option). Higher-end Synology models (e.g., DS1819+) offer stronger security and more bays if you need them.

Recommendation: If your external drive is already causing pain (running out of space or inconvenience backing up multiple devices), buying a NAS now is reasonable. Pick a beginner-friendly 2-bay if you want lower cost and simplicity, or a 4-bay (or higher) if you want more capacity and flexibility. Make sure the model you choose supports the encryption and access controls you care about.

If you want, tell me how much storage you currently need, your budget, and whether redundancy (RAID) matters to you and I can suggest specific models and a buying timeline.
